extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house counsel, and companies (especially software/startups) prosecuting or defending computer-implemented and business-method patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying the Supreme Court’s Section 101/Mayo framework to computer-implemented and business-method patent claims, with examples and prosecution recommendations. Focused on how courts determine whether claims are directed to abstract ideas and whether they include an ‘inventive concept.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-prong framework — prong one: directed to ineligible concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mayo framework asks two questions. First, are the claims at issue directed to 'abstract ideas,' 'laws of nature,' or 'natural phenomena,' each of which is categorically ineligible for patenting?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court has not provided a definitive definition of 'abstract idea'; it instead draws on prior decisions as examples (e.g., Benson: algorithm to convert binary-coded decimal to binary = abstract idea; Flook: mathematical formula for computing alarm limits = abstract idea; Bilski: method for hedging risk = fundamental economic concept). Every patent claim has an 'idea' at its core, so the initial inquiry is challenging and fact-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-prong framework — prong two: 'inventive concept' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Do the claims contain an "inventive concept" that is sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second prong examines whether claim elements, individually and 'as an ordered combination,' supply an inventive concept that transforms the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application. The Court stated that mere instructions to 'apply' an abstract idea are insufficient. Examples: In Alice, the Court found the claims did little more than tell practitioners to implement an abstract idea on a general-purpose computer and thus lacked an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Significantly more' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court requires that eligible patent claims must recite 'significantly more' than just the ineligible law of nature (or abstract idea) and routine applications thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion treats 'significantly more' as a necessary but unelaborated threshold—raising questions about how much additional material is needed. Practitioners must assess whether added claim limitations supply substantive technical contribution beyond the abstract concept and routine practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending an abstract idea with the words 'apply it' using a general-purpose computer is not enough to render a claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice held that steps like 'implement this abstract idea using a general-purpose computer' are insufficient. System and computer-readable medium claims that merely recite generic, conventional computer components for implementing the same abstract idea likewise fail prong two. Anti-pattern: claiming an abstract business concept and adding 'on a computer' without specific technical improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional, well-known steps at a high level of generality are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Appending conventional steps (i.e., steps 'well known in the art'), specified only at a high level of generality, does not supply the inventive concept required by Mayo prong two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo itself showed that adding conventional, routine activity described in broad terms will not transform an ineligible concept into a patentable application. Avoid high-level recitations of routine industry practices as purportedly inventive claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer functioning or another technology can support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that improve the functioning of the computer itself or effect an improvement in another technology or technical field may be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr illustrated that nonconventional application of technology (e.g., using a thermocouple in a particular way to improve rubber curing) supports eligibility. The Alice Court noted claims that 'purport to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or effect technological improvements are more likely to pass Section 101 analysis. Guidance for drafters: tie the invention to concrete technological improvements rather than abstruse business aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological-foundation / 'technological arts' consideration (higher scrutiny for business methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims having a more significant technological foundation are more likely to recite patentable subject matter; by contrast, business-method claims (pure 'business concepts') are more likely to be deemed abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Federal Circuit previously found the 'technological arts' test unworkable, Alice demonstrates the Court looks to technological aspects—whether claims address a technological problem or improve technology. Practitioners prosecuting business-method claims should consider expressly tying claims to technological improvements to reduce risk of invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims 'as an ordered combination' as well as element-by-element
rubrics_metrics.description: Mayo's second prong examines claim elements individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the combination supplies an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual elements are conventional, their particular ordered combination could supply an inventive concept—but in Alice viewing the claim as a whole still failed to supply the inventive concept. Drafters should consider whether a specific sequence or combination yields a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of hardware/computer components does not guarantee eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere presence of hardware and computerized functions in claims does not ensure patent eligibility if those elements are generic and conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice rejected system and medium claims because they merely recited generic and conventional computer components for implementing the same abstract idea as the method claim. Practitioners should avoid relying on token hardware recitations and instead specify concrete, nonconventional computer/architectural improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution drafting recommendation: lower abstraction and include implementation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may need to adopt claim-drafting techniques that target a lower level of abstraction, including incorporating implementation details into claims that illustrate an improvement of the functioning of a computer, technology, or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends incorporating implementation details, describing how the invention improves computer operation or other technology, and avoiding broad, high-level formulations of business methods. These tactical steps can help meet the Mayo 'inventive concept' requirement and fend off Section 101 challenges.
